concepts.name: Indo-Greek Bilingual and Biscriptal Coinage
key_dimensions: Use of Greek on obverse and Kharosthi/Brahmi on reverse — significance of bilingualism as administrative adaptation
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Kharosthi (Indo-Greek northwest) vs Brahmi (eastern Indo-Greek rulers like Agathocles) usage
First issuance of bilingual coins in Indian subcontinent — historiographical significance for reconstructing Indo-Greek history
Contrast with purely Greek or purely Indian coinage traditions to show cultural syncretism

concepts.name: Agathocles and the Earliest Indian Script Coins
key_dimensions: Agathocles identified as the first Indo-Greek ruler to use Brahmi script on coins — a frequent factual UPSC question
His coins also depicted Hindu and Buddhist iconography (Vasudeva-Krishna, Balarama-Samkarshana) — earliest numismatic evidence of these deities
Distinction between his Taxila-mint Kharosthi coins and his Brahmi coins — regional administrative logic
Significance as evidence for Indo-Greek interaction with indigenous religious traditions before Menander

concepts.name: Menander I (Milinda) and Buddhist Iconography on Coins
key_dimensions: Menander's coins bear the Dharmachakra symbol — numismatic corroboration of his Buddhist sympathies described in Milindapanha
UPSC trap: Not all Indo-Greek rulers used Buddhist symbols; Menander is the primary example — avoid overgeneralisation
His portrait coins introduced the 'heroic' bust style — Greek artistic convention adapted in Indian context
Coins as primary source for reconstructing Menander's vast kingdom given absence of literary Indian sources

concepts.name: Portrait Coinage Tradition of Indo-Greeks
key_dimensions: Indo-Greeks introduced realistic ruler portrait on obverse — a Hellenistic tradition absent in Mauryan punch-mark coins
Historiographical value: coins are the ONLY source for identifying many Indo-Greek rulers (e.g., over 30 rulers known only from coins)
UPSC trap: Mauryan coins (punch-mark) had NO royal portraits — contrast is a classic question angle
Portrait style evolution: early Hellenistic realism vs later schematised/Indianised portraits under later rulers

concepts.name: Round vs Square Coin Shapes among Indo-Greeks
key_dimensions: Indo-Greeks issued both round coins (Greek tradition) for western markets and square coins (Indian tradition) for local circulation — evidence of economic pragmatism
Square copper coins with Kharosthi legends targeted Indian populations; round silver coins targeted Hellenistic trade networks
UPSC trap: Square coins were NOT an Indo-Greek invention — indigenous Indian tradition pre-existed; Indo-Greeks adapted it
Bifurcation of coin shape by metal: silver typically round, copper typically square — important pattern

concepts.name: Metals Used in Indo-Greek and Kushana Coinage — Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Indo-Greeks primarily issued silver and copper; gold coinage was rare and limited (contrast with Kushanas)
Kushanas introduced prolific GOLD coinage (dināra) — reflects access to Central Asian gold trade routes and Roman trade surplus
UPSC trap: The shift from silver-dominant (Indo-Greek/Saka) to gold-dominant (Kushana) coinage marks a major economic transition
Debasement of Kushana gold under later rulers (post-Vasudeva I) — economic decline indicator

concepts.name: Kushana Gold Dināra and Roman Aureus Connection
key_dimensions: Kushana gold coin (dināra) weight and purity modelled on Roman aureus — evidence of Indo-Roman trade integration
Term 'dināra' itself derived from Latin 'denarius' via Parthian intermediary — linguistic-numismatic linkage
UPSC trap: Kushana dināra ≠ later Gupta dināra; Gupta gold coinage was inspired by but distinct from Kushana dināra
Roman coins found in South India vs Kushana dināra circulating in North/Northwest — geographic distribution question

concepts.name: Vima Kadphises and the Introduction of Kushana Gold Coinage
key_dimensions: Vima Kadphises credited with introducing large-scale gold coinage among Kushanas — marks economic maturation of the empire
His coins depict Shiva with trident and bull (Nandi) — earliest Kushana use of Shaivite iconography on coins
UPSC trap: Kujula Kadphises (founder) issued copper coins, NOT gold — the gold coinage began with Vima Kadphises
Coins of Vima bear Greek legend 'BASILEOS BASILEON SŌTĒROS' (King of Kings, Saviour) — continued Hellenistic titulature

concepts.name: Kanishka I's Coinage and Multi-Religious Iconography
key_dimensions: Kanishka's coins are unique for depicting deities from Greek, Iranian (Zoroastrian), Hindu AND Buddhist pantheons — unparalleled religious pluralism
His coins are among the earliest to depict the Buddha in human form with a label 'BODDO' — critical art history-numismatics overlap
UPSC trap: The Buddha image on Kanishka's coins predates or is contemporary with Gandhara sculptural Buddha — sequence is debated and frequently tested
Iranian deities (Mithra, Nana, Pharro) on Kanishka's coins — evidence of Kushana Central Asian cultural roots

concepts.name: Language Shift on Kushana Coins: Greek to Bactrian
key_dimensions: Early Kushana coins used Greek script/language (inherited from Indo-Greeks via Sakas); Kanishka I switched to Bactrian language written in Greek script
This shift marks assertion of Kushana cultural identity distinct from Hellenistic legacy
UPSC trap: Bactrian language ≠ Greek language; Bactrian is an Iranian language merely written in Greek alphabet on coins
Kanishka's coins retain Greek letters but the words are Iranian — a subtle but examinable distinction

concepts.name: Punch-Mark Coins vs Indo-Greek Die-Struck Coins — Technological Transition
key_dimensions: Mauryan/pre-Mauryan punch-mark coins were made by punching symbols on metal blanks; Indo-Greeks introduced die-striking technology to India
Die-striking allowed consistent portraiture and detailed iconography — explains superior artistic quality of Indo-Greek coins
UPSC trap: Die-struck coins ≠ mould-cast coins; cast coins were used by some local dynasties but Indo-Greeks used die-striking
This technological import had lasting impact — all subsequent Indian dynastic coinage (Satavahanas, Guptas) used die-striking

concepts.name: Saka-Pahlava Coinage as Transitional Link between Indo-Greeks and Kushanas
key_dimensions: Sakas and Pahlavas (Indo-Parthians) maintained bilingual coinage tradition of Indo-Greeks but gradually increased Indian iconographic elements
Gondophares (Indo-Parthian) coins — associated with St. Thomas Christian tradition; numismatic-historical crossover
UPSC trap: Sakas ≠ Kushanas; they are distinct Central Asian groups though often confused — coins help differentiate them
Maues (first major Saka king) coins continued Greek portrait tradition — shows cultural continuity despite political change

concepts.name: Iconography of Greek Deities on Indo-Greek Coins and Their Symbolic Meanings
key_dimensions: Athena Alkidemos (Athena the defender) — symbol on Menander's coins; became almost a dynastic emblem
Apollo, Zeus, Heracles on various Indo-Greek coins — each deity's selection reflected ruler's political messaging
UPSC trap: The goddess on the reverse of Indo-Greek coins is NOT always the same deity — different rulers chose different patron deities
Gradual replacement of Greek deities by Indian deities on later Indo-Greek coins — measurable index of Indianisation

concepts.name: Coins as Primary Historical Source for Post-Mauryan Northwest India
key_dimensions: For Indo-Greeks, coins are virtually the ONLY indigenous source — no contemporary Indian literary source names most rulers
Numismatic evidence used to establish chronology, territorial extent, and synchronisation with Classical sources (Strabo, Justin)
UPSC trap: Milindapanha mentions Menander but is a Buddhist text, not a political chronicle — coins provide independent corroboration
Overstrike evidence on coins helps establish relative chronology between rulers — a methodological point

concepts.name: Kushana Coinage and Evidence for Trade with Rome
key_dimensions: High gold purity of Kushana dināra maintained to facilitate trade with Rome — purity as trade policy instrument
Hoard distribution of Kushana coins along Silk Route and in South Indian ports — maps actual trade circuits
UPSC trap: Roman coins found in India ≠ direct evidence of Roman political presence; it indicates trade, not conquest
Kushana coinage decline in gold purity post-3rd century CE correlates with decline of Roman trade — economic interdependence

concepts.name: Huvishka's Coinage and the Widest Pantheon of Deities
key_dimensions: Huvishka's coins show the largest number of deities of any Kushana ruler — over 30 different divine figures identified
Includes Shaivite, Vaishnavite, Buddhist, Greek, and Iranian deities simultaneously — peak of Kushana religious syncretism
UPSC trap: This religious plurality on coins does NOT mean Huvishka was irreligious — it reflects imperial policy of inclusion
Art historical significance: Huvishka coins provide visual vocabulary for Kushana religious art of the period

concepts.name: Wima Takto (Soter Megas) Coinage — The Anonymous King Problem
key_dimensions: Coins bearing title 'Soter Megas' (Great Saviour) but NO personal name — long debated anonymous Kushana ruler
Modern scholarship (based on Rabatak inscription) identifies him as Vima Takto — shows how epigraphy resolves numismatic puzzles
UPSC trap: 'Soter Megas' is a TITLE not a name — a classic trap in objective questions
His coins show the king on horseback — military iconography distinct from frontal standing figures on later Kushana coins

concepts.name: Debasement and Decline of Kushana Coinage Post-Vasudeva I
key_dimensions: Post-Vasudeva I Kushana coins show progressive reduction in gold content — numismatic evidence for political-economic decline
Coincides with Sassanid pressure from west and emergence of regional powers — multi-causal decline
UPSC trap: Kushana empire did not end abruptly; 'Kushano-Sassanid' coins represent a transitional hybrid phase
Comparison with Gupta gold coins: Gupta dināra maintained higher purity — implies stronger economic base of early Gupta empire

concepts.name: Numismatic Evidence for Kushana Ruler Chronology and the 'Kanishka Era' Debate
key_dimensions: No consensus on the starting date of Kanishka's era (78 CE, 128 CE, and other dates proposed) — coins alone cannot resolve this
Coins provide RELATIVE chronology (who came before/after) but not ABSOLUTE dates without external synchronisation
UPSC trap: The Saka era (78 CE) is often confused with Kanishka's era — they are distinct and the confusion is a standard trap
Cross-referencing coin hoards, stratigraphy, and Chinese sources used to triangulate Kushana chronology — interdisciplinary method

concepts.name: Local Imitation and Counterfeit Coinage — Indo-Greek Influence on Indigenous Dynasties
key_dimensions: Indian Kshatrapa rulers, Audumbaras, Kunindas issued coins imitating Indo-Greek style — measures of cultural diffusion
Tribal coins of Kunindas (Uttarakhand) show Indo-Greek portrait influence combined with local symbols (deer, goddess)
UPSC trap: Imitation coins ≠ direct Indo-Greek rule; they indicate cultural influence in regions Indo-Greeks may not have controlled
This diffusion of coinage culture to tribal/regional polities is significant for understanding post-Mauryan political decentralisation
